subject: Specifying fixed effects priors for sites in survey data

messages.author: 725d9567da763691
messages.subject: Specifying fixed effects priors for sites in survey data
parts:
Hi,

I'm running a binomial spde model for multiple species across multiple sites. I am interested in site level effects and interactions with a year effect (continuous variable). Some species have very low or zero presence at some sites and this seems to cause issues with estimates for site level effects and interactions and interpretation of these effects.

I note that the default prior for fixed effects is (0, 0.001). I have tried altering the precision and this has a profound (perhaps expected) effect on my estimates. I have included output below where I use a precision of 0.1,  0.01, 0.001 and 0.0001. I have used expand.factor.strategy = 'inla' in order to get estimates for all sites.

If I run the model as a glm without any latent effects I note that I have very large standard errors for sites and interactions where this example species is absent (Beagle and Huon) - see last output. This is a different model specification with treatment contrats, but I think the principle holds true. So, it seems that I require a large variance in those cases, and smaller when the species is present. 

Is there a prior that would better suit than the default here? When I run the model for a different species the sites with high/zero abundance will change so I'd rather have something that could be used for all species.

TIA

Nick

   c("inla(formula = inla.spt.form, family = \"binomial\", data = inla.stack.data(stack), ", " Ntrials = ntrial,

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Specifying fixed effects priors for sites in survey data
parts:
Hi,

if you use expand.factor.strategy = 'inla', you are kind of asking for
large marginal stdev's, as it do the expansion so you, by purpose,
create confounding, so only certain contrasts are likelihood
identifiable.

I see your concern as you want one coefficient for each effect. By
default lm() and glm() remove one level of the factor to make it
likelihood identifiable. Another approach is this one, which might be
what you want.

H
